title: Voters approve $1.83 billion Portland Public Schools bond
author: Julia Silverman
summary: Election-night report (updated the next morning) that Portland voters approved the $1.83 billion PPS bond, 58% to 42% in partial returns, a narrower margin than the 3-to-1 approval of the 2020 bond. About $1.15 billion goes to modernization, with roughly $974 million projected for Jefferson, Cleveland and Wells high schools, each designed for 1,700 students at $430-466 million apiece. COO Dan Jung, leaving in June, said updated high school estimates and any savings for elementary and middle schools would not be known until summer. The rebuilt schools would give 15,300 high school seats against a PSU projection of about 10,700 high school students by 2039; Armstrong said extra space could be repurposed, while leaders including chair Eddie Wang framed the projects as a bet on the city's future. The bond also carries $190 million for K-8 maintenance, with at least $90 million pledged to seismic work at the 8-10 highest-risk unreinforced masonry schools.

title: External Auditor Finds PPS Bond Program Is at Heightened Risk of Fraud
author: Joanna Hou
summary: WW obtained a draft audit by PPS's longtime external auditor, Sjoberg Evashenk Consulting, concluding the $1.83 billion 2025 bond program faces heightened fraud risk because PPS outsourced program management to Texas-based Procedeo under a $61.5 million contract without adequate oversight. The draft's four findings say PPS lacked a sound business case, risked favoritism in selection, overpaid relative to market, failed to review invoices, and cut much of its in-house modernization staff on Procedeo's advice, creating a conflict and losing institutional knowledge. Auditors say leadership overstated the old office's problems to the board, and that the board did not adequately scrutinize the contract. PPS says the draft is unfinished and it disagrees with some findings but is making improvements; Procedeo defended its work. Earlier bonds were found generally sound.
key_facts: Draft audit covers the $1.83 billion 2025 bond rebuilding three high schools; Procedeo contract is $61.5 million.
Four findings and 38 recommendations; PPS staff preparing responses.
Auditors found overpayments to Procedeo of more than $762,000 due to insufficient invoice review.
About half of the Office of School Modernization's 30 employees were terminated in January on Procedeo's recommendation, per the report.
Auditors found about $193,400 in unallowable bond project costs and nearly $1 million in unsupported payroll charges.
Procedeo joined the bond program in December 2025, per its CEO.
Auditors said PPS generally met obligations on its 2012, 2017 and 2020 bonds and is 'off to a good start' with the 2025 bond.
PPS spokesperson: ground broken on two high school modernizations this year, a third to follow in November.
Audit recommends renegotiating the Procedeo contract and rebuilding internal bond-management capacity.

title: Portland School Board Responds to External Bond Auditor

summary: The Portland School Board drafted its response to the 10 recommendations directed at it in the external audit of PPS's bond program, with a majority concurring with each. title: Portland Public Schools issues a combative response to critical bond audit

summary: PPS released the final external bond audit by Sjoberg Evashenk along with a pointed management response. title: Editorial: A PPS board breakdown signals bad news for the public
author: The Oregonian Editorial Board
summary: The editorial board argues the Dec. 2, 2025 meeting approving the Procedeo construction management contract showed a chair who cannot run a meeting, a superintendent resistant to questions and a board near breakdown. It faults DePass for decrying '13 years of failures' while ignoring on-time modernizations, Wang for letting the audience jeer directors and for ending debate after about 45 minutes to cut off Engelsman's questions, and Armstrong for disparaging her own Office of School Modernization staff. title: With enrollment declining and costs going up, Portland Public Schools tightens its belt — again

summary: Superintendent Armstrong presented a 2025-26 budget of about $1.09 billion, only ~1.4% above the current year, leaving a roughly $40 million gap blamed on an 11% enrollment drop since 2019 and rising pay, benefits and inflation. title: Plans emerge for pared-back high schools in Portland

summary: After the board told project managers in February 2025 to trim the Jefferson, Cleveland and Wells modernizations (each estimated well over $400 million) to about 295,000 square feet, newly released Office of School Modernization documents outlined possible cuts so savings could go to elementary and middle school maintenance. At Jefferson, designers proposed halving the theater from 1,000 to 500 seats, smaller choir and dance rooms, and dropping community partner, team, mediation and student government spaces. At Wells, ideas included a smaller band room, two fewer CTE classrooms, no teen parent center and less flexible space; at Cleveland, about 23,000 square feet less, including three classrooms and a science lab, plus lower contractor fees. title: Oregon public school enrollment levels off, with no sign of rebound from deep post-pandemic losses
author: Julia Silverman
summary: Oregon Department of Education fall 2024 counts show statewide enrollment down about 2,300 students (0.4%) from 2023-24, a smaller drop than in prior years but with no recovery toward pre-pandemic levels. PPS lost about 660 students (1.5%) to roughly 43,300, a steeper decline than the state's, which reduces its share of state per-pupil funding; the district was planning about $40 million in cuts for the next year. PSU demographers attribute declines to falling birth rates and high housing costs driving out-migration, with the smallest cohorts in early elementary grades. Among metro districts, West Linn-Wilsonville and Parkrose also fell faster than the state, while David Douglas, Gresham-Barlow and Estacada grew slightly. The article notes school-closure talk had not spread widely: West Linn-Wilsonville shelved consolidation amid parent opposition and Beaverton paused its discussion for 18 months of community conversations.

title: Closing schools could save about $1 million per building, Portland Public Schools superintendent says

summary: The Portland School Board unanimously renamed Jason Lee Elementary in East Portland as Sunrise Elementary. summary: OPB compares the closure processes in Portland and Salem-Keizer, which together could close up to 20 schools, noting common features (family opposition, budget gaps, a gubernatorial response, Chiefs for Change claims) and differences. For PPS it reports concerns from the Special Education PTSA that receiving schools may lack space for students with disabilities, and a Lewis Elementary parent's frustration after an after-school conversation with board chair Eddie Wang and member Michelle DePass, which she called performative; Armstrong later visited Lewis with two other board members. The piece notes Armstrong opened a recent board meeting with a slide saying closures are about concentrating resources, not cutting the deficit, and that PPS did not use FLO Analytics for closures but relied on internal data, PSU's Population Research Center and an equity audit.
